t.3.41.1: That lovely-hipped lady, while gathering flowers, caught sight of him, adorned with flanks the colour of gold and silver.
t.3.41.2: And the delighted lady of flawless limbs, her complexion like burnished gold, called out to her husband and also to Lakṣmaṇa, who bore his weapons.
t.3.41.3: Summoned by her, Vaidehī, those tigers among men, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, then looked over that place and saw the deer.
t.3.41.4: But Lakṣmaṇa, growing suspicious on seeing it, said to Rāma: "I think this deer is none other than that very rākṣasa Mārīca."
t.3.41.5: O Rāma, kings who roamed the forest joyfully on the hunt have been slain by this wicked one, who takes any form at will, through his deceitful guise.
t.3.41.6: O radiant tiger among men, this illusory deer-form, like a city of the gandharvas, has been fashioned by this master of illusion.
t.3.41.7: For such a deer, dappled with jewels, does not exist in the world, O Rāghava, O lord of the earth; this is surely an illusion, there is no doubt.
t.3.41.8: As Kākutstha was speaking thus, Sītā of the bright smile, her mind stolen away by the deception, checked him and, thrilled with delight, spoke.
t.3.41.9: My noble lord, that charming deer steals my heart. Bring it here, O mighty-armed one; it will be a plaything for us.
t.3.41.11: O mighty-armed one, bears, herds of spotted deer, monkeys and Kiṃnaras likewise roam here, excellent in form and of great strength.
t.3.41.10: Here at our hermitage many deer of auspicious appearance roam together, and so too do yaks and sṛmara deer.
t.3.41.12: O king, never before has a deer been seen that is equal to this one in splendor, in forbearance and in radiance, as is this most excellent of deer.
t.3.41.13: With limbs variegated in many colours and studded with gem-like spots, it shines like the moon, illuminating the tranquil forest.
t.3.41.14: Ah, what beauty! Ah, what splendor! And how lovely is the richness of its voice! That wondrous, many-hued deer seems to steal my heart away.
t.3.41.15: If this deer comes into your grasp while still alive, it will be a marvel and will fill everyone with wonder.
t.3.41.16: When our dwelling in the forest is completed and we are once more established in the kingdom, this deer will serve as an ornament for the inner apartments.
t.3.41.18: If this finest of deer does not come into your grasp alive, O tiger among men, its beautiful hide will be mine.
t.3.41.17: O lord, this divine form of a deer will awaken wonder in the noble prince Bharata, in my mothers-in-law, and in me.
t.3.41.19: When this creature has been slain, I wish to sit upon its golden skin, spread out over a cushion of tender grass.
t.3.41.20: This conduct driven by desire is harsh and is thought unbecoming for women; yet the beauty of this creature has awakened wonder in me.
t.3.41.21: Because of that creature, with its golden hair and horns of the finest gems, its hue like the young sun and its splendour like the path of the stars, even Rāghava's mind was filled with wonder.
t.3.41.22: Having heard these words of Sītā and having seen the wondrous deer, Rāghava, delighted, spoke these words to his brother Lakṣmaṇa.
t.3.41.24: Neither in the grove of Nandana nor in the shelter of Caitraratha is there any deer that is equal to this one; how then on earth, O Saumitri?
t.3.41.23: Look, Lakṣmaṇa, at this longing of Vaidehī that has fixed itself upon the deer. Because of its surpassing beauty, this deer will not survive today.
t.3.41.25: The lovely lines of hair on the deer, some lying against the grain and some with it, variegated with drops of gold, shine forth as they cover its body.
t.3.41.26: Look at his blazing tongue, like a tongue of fire, issuing from his mouth as he yawns, like lightning flashing out from a cloud.
t.3.41.27: With its face of sapphire and crystal and its belly gleaming like conch-shell and pearl, whose heart, indeed, would this lovely deer not captivate?
t.3.41.28: Whose mind would not be filled with wonder on seeing this form, radiant with the lustre of jāmbūnada gold, made of many kinds of gems, and divine?
t.3.41.29: O Lakṣmaṇa, kings wielding bows slay deer while hunting in the great forest, both for the sake of their flesh and for sport.
t.3.41.30: Through diligent effort, riches are gathered in the great forest, and minerals of many kinds as well, containing gems, jewels and gold.
t.3.41.32: That object which a seeker, bent on the work of gaining his aim, goes after without hesitation, O Lakṣmaṇa, is what those versed in the science of wealth and those wise in worldly gain call true wealth.
t.3.41.31: That whole essence of men's wealth, which swells their store, everything conceived in the mind, is like the wealth of Śukra, O Lakṣmaṇa.
t.3.41.33: On the precious golden skin of this jewel among deer, slender-waisted Vaidehī will sit together with me.
t.3.41.35: This splendid deer here, and that divine one which roams the sky, both these deer are divine: the star-deer and the earth-deer.
t.3.41.34: Neither a kādalī hide, nor a priyakī hide, nor a praveṇī blanket, nor yet an āvikī of sheep's wool could equal this one in its touch; such is my opinion.
t.3.41.36: Or if this should be as you tell me, Lakṣmaṇa, that this is the illusion of a rākṣasa, then its slaying must be carried out by me.
t.3.41.37: For it was by this cruel Mārīca, of unrestrained mind, roaming in the forest, that the foremost of sages were slain in former times.
t.3.41.39: Formerly, here, Vātāpi, having humiliated the ascetics, would kill the brahmins while lodged in their bellies, just as its own foetus kills a she-mule.
t.3.41.38: This creature has sprung up during the hunt and slain many kings, great archers, so this deer must surely be killed.
t.3.41.40: Once, after a long time in the world, he came upon the great sage Agastya, endowed with spiritual power, and became food for him.
t.3.41.41: Seeing him eager to take on that form again in order to rise up, the blessed one smiled and said this to Vātāpi.
t.3.41.42: O Vātāpi, heedlessly you overpowered with your might the foremost of the twice-born in the world of living beings; therefore you have come to decay.
t.3.41.43: Thus, O Lakṣmaṇa, that rākṣasa who would scorn one like me, ever devoted to dharma and master of his senses, would cease to exist, just like Vātāpi.
t.3.41.44: This Vātāpi would be slain as if by Agastya, for his course leads him to me. You stay here, armed and self-restrained, and guard Maithilī.
t.3.41.45: O Raghunandana, whatever task is ours depends upon her; I shall either kill this deer or capture it.
t.3.41.46: While I go swiftly, O Saumitri, to bring back the deer, watch over Vaidehī, O Lakṣmaṇa, whose heart is set on the deer's skin.
t.3.41.47: For today this deer, prized for its splendid hide, shall not survive. You must remain vigilant, staying in the hermitage with Sītā.
t.3.41.48: Until I slay the spotted deer with a single arrow, O Lakṣmaṇa; having slain it and taken this hide, I shall swiftly return.
t.3.41.49: O Lakṣmaṇa, together with the bird Jaṭāyus, who is skillful, exceedingly strong and wise, take Maithilī into your care and remain vigilant, wary on every side at every moment.
